title: Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective
claim: Existing time-domain tokenizers distort the underlying signal's spectrum through aliasing, while shifting spectral bands to baseband preserves it.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, time domain vs frequency domain, arrow showing shift
description: Two side-by-side plots. The left plot shows a noisy sinusoidal time series, amplitude against time, with a dark curve oscillating over several periods. A narrow green dashed window marks a patch token, with dense green dots crowded on one steep segment of the curve. Red dots spaced evenly across the whole series are joined by a nearly flat red line, labeled phase token. Bold green and red text labels sit next to each. The right plot shows the frequency spectrum, with a sharp peak near zero. Two shaded purple bands are marked by dashed lines, with purple dots in the higher band. A large arrow points left from the higher band to the baseband, labeled Spectral Shifting. Purple text reads TimeFT (one block). A B label sits on the frequency axis.
caption: The key distinction between existing tokenization and TimeFT. Left: The processes of patch and phase tokenization in the time domain. Right: Spectral shifting moves the frequency spectrum, preventing aliasing by ensuring all components satisfy the Nyquist criterion.
abstract: Tokenization that partitions time series into subsequences has become a foundational paradigm in modern time series modeling. However, we find that current tokenization strategies inherently introduce spectral distortions, forcing the learned representations to diverge from the true underlying patterns such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, thereby impairing model performance. Through theoretical analysis from a frequency perspective, we derive the boundary conditions under which such distortions occur. To overcome this distortion, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data. TimeFT obtains tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting, and Nyquist sampling. The method is parameter-free, incurs negligible computational complexity, and can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizers. Our extensive experiments on diverse tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that TimeFT consistently and significantly improves performance.
